simple: one running sequence of instructions inside a program; a program can have several.
analogy: one chef's list of tickets.
precise: an independent flow of control with its own registers, program counter and stack, sharing the address space of its process; the operating system schedules threads onto cores (F2-34, F3-03).
source: D3 of F1-30 (Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the C++ object that starts a thread and lets you wait for it.
analogy: the name card of one cook, which the head chef keeps until that cook is done.
precise: a class in <thread> whose constructor starts a new thread of execution running a callable with copies of the given arguments; the object represents that thread until it is joined or detached.
source: D1 of F2-34 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): clause [intro.multithread] "Multi-threaded executions and data races"); D2 of F2-34 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: wait until a thread has finished.
analogy: waiting until a cook's tray is on the pass.
precise: join() blocks the calling thread until the thread represented by the object has completed; everything the finished thread did happens-before the return from join() (F2-39), so its results can be read safely afterwards.
source: D1 of F2-34 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): clause [intro.multithread] "Multi-threaded executions and data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: let a thread run on its own; nobody will wait for it.
analogy: sending a cook off without asking for the tray back.
precise: detach() separates the thread of execution from the std::thread object; the thread keeps running and its resources are released when it ends; nothing in the program can wait for it any more.
source: D1 of F2-34 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): clause [intro.multithread] "Multi-threaded executions and data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "still has a thread that somebody must wait for or let go".
analogy: the head chef still holds the cook's name card.
precise: a std::thread is joinable if it represents a thread of execution (it was started and neither joined nor detached); destroying a joinable std::thread calls std::terminate().
source: D1 of F2-34 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): clause [intro.multithread] "Multi-threaded executions and data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a thread object that joins itself when it goes away and can be asked politely to stop.
analogy: a cook who, at closing time, is told "please stop" and is then waited for automatically.
precise: a C++20 class in <thread> like std::thread, whose destructor calls request_stop() and then join(); it owns a stop source and passes a std::stop_token to a callable that accepts one.
source: D1 of F2-34 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): clause [intro.multithread] "Multi-threaded executions and data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: concurrency means several jobs are in progress at once; parallelism means several jobs are being worked on at the same instant.
analogy: one cook switching between three pots is concurrency; three cooks each stirring a pot is parallelism.
precise: concurrency is a property of the program's structure (several threads whose executions overlap in time); parallelism needs hardware that runs them simultaneously (several cores, F1-30).
source: D3 of F2-34 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?"); D7 of F2-34 (Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many times faster the job got.
analogy: the wedding order took a quarter of the time with four cooks: speedup 4.
precise: the time of the best one-thread version divided by the time of the parallel version, measured on the same machine; Amdahl's law (F1-30) bounds it.
source: D3 of F2-34 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: some threads get much more work than others, so everyone waits for the slowest.
analogy: one cook gets all the difficult dumplings.
precise: the situation where the work assigned to threads is unequal, so the parallel time is set by the most loaded thread rather than by the average.
source: D3 of F2-34 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one variable's worth of memory that the rules about threads talk about.
analogy: one order slip on the wall.
precise: an object of scalar type (an int, a pointer, a bool…) or a maximal sequence of adjacent non-zero-width bit-fields; two threads may update different memory locations without interfering, even if they are neighbours in memory.
source: D1 of F2-35 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [intro.memory] (memory locations), [intro.races] "Data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two uses of the same variable where at least one changes it.
analogy: one cook reads the slip while another rewrites it.
precise: two expression evaluations conflict if one of them modifies a memory location and the other reads or modifies the same memory location.
source: D1 of F2-35 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [intro.memory] (memory locations), [intro.races] "Data races") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two threads touching the same memory at the same time, at least one writing, with nothing to keep them in order.
analogy: two chefs updating the lemon board at once.
precise: in C++, two conflicting accesses to the same memory location from different threads, at least one a write, not ordered by synchronisation and not both atomic; a program with a data race has undefined behaviour.
source: D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one thread's change is overwritten as if it never happened.
analogy: two plates out, the slip went up by one.
precise: the outcome of interleaved read–modify–write sequences in which a thread stores a value computed from a stale read, erasing another thread's store.
source: D3 of F2-35 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?"); D7 of F2-35 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one possible order in which the steps of several threads happen.
analogy: who reads the lemon board first.
precise: a total order of the memory operations of concurrent threads that respects each thread's own order; different runs can produce different interleavings.
source: D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a bug where the result depends on which thread gets there first.
analogy: two cooks both see "one portion left" and both promise it to a table.
precise: a correctness bug that occurs only under some timings of concurrent operations; it may involve a data race, or happen with every access properly synchronised (a check-then-act on an atomic, F2-38).
source: D2 of F2-35 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action"); D3 of F2-35 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a compiler option that adds checks to your program so that it reports data races while it runs.
analogy: a supervisor who watches every slip and writes down every time two cooks touch one without taking turns.
precise: a dynamic data-race detector in GCC and Clang, enabled with -fsanitize=thread; it instruments memory accesses and synchronisation and reports pairs of conflicting accesses that were not ordered by happens-before in the execution that ran.
source: D5 of F2-35 (ThreadSanitizer documentation: the Clang/LLVM "ThreadSanitizer") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a lock that only one thread can hold at a time.
analogy: the single key to the spice cabinet.
precise: a mutual-exclusion object; lock() blocks until the calling thread owns it, unlock() releases it; an unlock of a mutex synchronises with the next successful lock of the same mutex, so it creates happens-before (F2-35). std::mutex is in <mutex>.
source: D1 of F2-36 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [thread.mutex] "Mutual exclusion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the piece of code that runs while the lock is held.
analogy: the time between taking the key and hanging it back.
precise: a region of code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time; a mutex enforces this by being held for the whole region.
source: D7 of F2-36 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fact about the data that is true whenever nobody holds the lock.
analogy: "the stock list matches the jars" whenever the key is on its hook.
precise: a condition (MA102, F2-09) that may be broken temporarily inside a critical section but must hold at every lock and unlock; it is what the mutex really protects.
source: D2 of F2-36 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an object that locks a mutex when created and unlocks it when it goes away.
analogy: a key on a spring that flies back to its hook when you leave the room.
precise: an RAII class template whose constructor calls lock() and whose destructor calls unlock(), also when the scope is left by return or by an exception.
source: D1 of F2-36 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [thread.mutex] "Mutual exclusion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a more flexible lock holder that can unlock early, relock, or be moved.
analogy: a key you may hang back early and take again.
precise: an RAII lock owner that may or may not own its mutex at a given moment; supports deferred locking, try_lock, timed locking, unlock()/lock() and move; required by std::condition_variable (F2-37).
source: D1 of F2-36 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [thread.mutex] "Mutual exclusion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a lock holder that can take several mutexes at once without deadlocking.
analogy: taking the spice key and the fridge key together, in a way that never leaves two cooks each holding one.
precise: a C++17 RAII class template that locks zero or more mutexes using the deadlock-avoidance algorithm of std::lock and unlocks them in its destructor (F2-40).
source: D1 of F2-36 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [thread.mutex] "Mutual exclusion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a lock that many readers may hold together, but a writer only alone.
analogy: anyone may read the menu board at once; changing it needs everyone to step back.
precise: std::shared_mutex (<shared_mutex>) has exclusive ownership (lock, used through std::unique_lock) and shared ownership (lock_shared, used through std::shared_lock); shared owners exclude exclusive ones.
source: D1 of F2-36 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20): [thread.mutex] "Mutual exclusion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: threads waiting for the same lock instead of working.
analogy: a queue of cooks in front of the key hook.
precise: the situation in which several threads try to acquire the same lock at the same time; contended acquisitions cost far more than uncontended ones and serialise the critical sections.
source: D3 of F2-36 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: something a thread can sleep on until another thread says "something changed".
analogy: the bell at the pass.
precise: a synchronisation object (std::condition_variable, header <condition_variable>) with wait, which atomically unlocks a std::unique_lock<std::mutex> and blocks, and relocks before returning; and notify_one/notify_all, which unblock waiting threads. It carries no state of its own.
source: D1 of F2-37 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the yes/no question the waiting thread really cares about, such as "is there a plate?".
analogy: looking at the pass after the bell.
precise: a callable returning bool, evaluated with the mutex held; cv.wait(lock, pred) is equivalent to while (!pred()) cv.wait(lock);.
source: D1 of F2-37 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a wait that returns although nobody notified, or although the condition is false again.
analogy: you hear a bell, but the plate is gone or there never was one.
precise: the standard allows wait to return without a corresponding notification; and between a notification and the waiter's relock, another thread may change the state. Both are handled by re-checking the predicate.
source: D1 of F2-37 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a notification sent when nobody was waiting, so nobody gets it.
analogy: the bell rang before the waiter arrived.
precise: because a condition variable has no memory, a notify with no waiting thread has no effect; a thread that waits afterwards without first checking the state may block for ever.
source: D2 of F2-37 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: some threads make items, others use them, and a fixed-size shelf sits between them.
analogy: the chef, the pass with four places, the waiters.
precise: a pattern in which producers insert into and consumers remove from a shared buffer of fixed capacity; producers block when it is full, consumers when it is empty. The block on "full" gives back-pressure: fast producers are slowed to the consumers' pace.
source: D7 of F2-37 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the next stage is too slow, the earlier stage is made to wait instead of piling up work.
analogy: when the pass is full, the chef stops plating.
precise: flow control in a pipeline in which a bounded buffer blocks or rejects producers, keeping memory use bounded.
source: D3 of F2-37 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed row of slots used in a circle: the writer adds at the head, the reader takes from the tail.
analogy: the shelf beside the door.
precise: a circular FIFO queue in an array with head and tail indices that wrap modulo its size; with one producer (the handler) and one consumer (the main program) it decouples arrival from processing.
source: D8, R2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D8 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an operation that happens all at once: no other thread can see it half done.
analogy: the pantry key: whoever holds it reads and writes the board before anyone else may.
precise: an operation on an atomic object that is indivisible with respect to other threads; for example std::atomic<long>::fetch_add, an atomic read-modify-write.
source: D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: read the register, change only your bits, write it back.
analogy: moving only your own jar on a shared shelf.
precise: an update sequence that preserves bits the software does not own (including reserved bits whose value must be preserved); it is not atomic unless the hardware or a lock makes it so.
source: C1 of F1-41 (pending verification)

simple: "change this to X, but only if it is still Y".
analogy: you set the counter to 50 only if it still shows the 42 you saw.
precise: an RMW that compares an atomic object with an expected value and, if equal, stores a desired value; otherwise it loads the current value into the expected variable. In C++: compare_exchange_strong and compare_exchange_weak (which may fail spuriously).
source: D1 of F2-38 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the atomic is done with special processor instructions, not with a hidden lock.
analogy: the counter is a real mechanical counter, not a clerk behind a door.
precise: std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free (compile time) and is_lock_free() (run time) report whether operations on the type never use a lock in the implementation; large types may be implemented with a lock.
source: D1 of F2-38 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a lock where a waiting thread keeps trying in a loop instead of sleeping.
analogy: a cook who stands at the cabinet trying the handle again and again.
precise: a mutual-exclusion lock built from an atomic flag; acquisition busy-waits on the flag; cheap for very short critical sections when the owner is running on another core, wasteful otherwise.
source: D3 of F2-38 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sequence of steps that must happen together but can be interrupted between steps.
analogy: look at the seat counter, see 999, turn away, then click: someone else clicked in between.
precise: a race condition (F2-35) in which a code region assumed to be indivisible is interleaved with conflicting operations of another thread; it can occur with atomic variables only, so it is not a data race and race detectors do not report it.
source: D5 of F2-38 (ThreadSanitizer documentation (Clang and GCC) and K. Serebryany, T. Iskhodzhanov, "ThreadSanitizer: data race detection in practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two threads slow each other down by writing different variables that happen to share one cache line.
analogy: two recipes printed on one sheet.
precise: coherence traffic caused by independent data items located in the same line; because coherence works per line, writes to either item invalidate the other core's copy of the whole line.
source: D1 of F1-36 (Bryant and O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D3 of F1-36 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rules that say which values a read in one thread may see from writes in other threads.
analogy: the kitchen's written rules about what the assistant may reorder.
precise: for C++, the part of the standard ([intro.multithread], [atomics.order]) that defines data races, happens-before and the values atomic loads may return; for hardware, the memory consistency model of the ISA (F1-37).
source: D1 of F2-39 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "this action is guaranteed to be finished and visible before that one".
analogy: the plate was down before the waiter looked, and the waiter knows it.
precise: a partial order on actions built from sequenced-before (program order in one thread) and synchronises-with (between threads), closed under transitivity. If a write happens-before a read of the same location, with no other write in between, the read sees that write.
source: D1 of F2-39 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the link between two threads that creates happens-before.
analogy: the waiter seeing the flag the chef raised.
precise: a release operation on an atomic object synchronises with an acquire operation on the same object that reads the value written by the release (or by a later write in its release sequence); unlock/lock of a mutex and thread start/join also synchronise.
source: D1 of F2-39 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one-way orderings: a release store keeps earlier work before it, an acquire load keeps later work after it.
analogy: "finish the dish, then flip the ready sign" / "see the sign, then pick up the dish".
precise: in C++, a release store that is read by an acquire load synchronises with it, so writes before the release happen-before reads after the acquire; it does not order a release store with a later acquire load to a different variable.
source: D6 of F1-37 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++ standard draft)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an atomic operation that is indivisible but orders nothing else.
analogy: the tally counter clicks correctly, but nobody may conclude anything about the plates from its number.
precise: memory_order_relaxed: the operation is atomic and respects the object's modification order, but creates no synchronises-with edge.
source: D1 of F2-39 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the result is as if all threads took turns, one memory operation at a time, each in program order.
analogy: one pen on a chain at the board; every cook writes and reads only with it.
precise: a model in which the result of any execution equals some single total order of all memory operations that respects each thread's program order (SC).
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D3 of F1-37 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an instruction that stops later memory operations from overtaking earlier ones.
analogy: "pin it up and wait before you look".
precise: an instruction (or language construct) that orders memory operations before it with those after it; on a TSO machine, a full fence drains the store buffer before later loads execute.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence"); D7 of F1-37 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: threads waiting for each other in a circle, so none can ever continue.
analogy: two cooks, each holding one key and waiting for the other's.
precise: a state in which every thread of a set is blocked waiting for a resource held by another thread of the same set; with mutexes, a cycle in the wait-for graph.
source: D7 of F2-40 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: four things that must all be true for a deadlock to happen.
analogy: keys are exclusive; cooks keep one key while waiting; nobody snatches keys; and the waiting forms a circle.
precise: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait (Coffman, Elphick, Shoshani, 1971); breaking any one prevents deadlock.
source: D7 of F2-40 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D12 of F2-40 (E. G. Coffman, M. Elphick, A. Shoshani, "System Deadlocks") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule saying in which order locks must be taken when you need more than one.
analogy: "spice key before fridge key, always".
precise: a total (or partial) order on locks such that every thread acquires locks only in increasing order; it makes circular wait impossible.
source: D2 of F2-40 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one piece of code takes A then B, another takes B then A.
analogy: Joon takes spices then fridge; Andrés fridge then spices.
precise: two acquisition paths that take the same pair of locks in opposite orders; a potential deadlock even if it has never occurred, because a suitable interleaving produces a cycle.
source: D5 of F2-40 (ThreadSanitizer documentation (Clang and GCC): deadlock detector, "lock-order-inversion") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a drawing with an arrow from each waiting thread to the thread it waits for.
analogy: "Joon waits for Andrés, Andrés waits for Joon": a circle on paper.
precise: a directed graph whose vertices are threads and with an edge T → U when T is blocked on a resource held by U; a deadlock is a cycle in it.
source: D7 of F2-40 (Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a snapshot of where every thread of a running program is, function by function.
analogy: a photo of the kitchen showing who is standing where and holding what.
precise: the call stack of every thread of a process, here taken with GDB by attaching to the process (gdb -p) and running thread apply all bt.
source: D13 of F2-40 ("Debugging with GDB") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: threads keep reacting to each other and so never get anything done, though none is blocked.
analogy: two cooks in a narrow corridor stepping aside the same way again and again.
precise: a state in which threads change state repeatedly in response to each other without making progress, for example when each releases its locks and retries in lock step.
source: D3 of F2-40 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an object that will hold a result that is not ready yet.
analogy: the numbered receipt the guest holds.
precise: std::future<T> (header <future>) is the reading end of a shared state; get() blocks until the value (or an exception) is stored, then returns it (or throws it); it can be called once. wait_for waits with a time limit.
source: D1 of F2-41 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the writing end that a thread uses to deliver a future's value.
analogy: the cook's copy of the receipt, handed in with the dish.
precise: std::promise<T> owns a shared state; get_future() returns the matching future; set_value/set_exception make it ready; setting it synchronises with the future's get.
source: D1 of F2-41 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a function wrapped so that calling it fills a future.
analogy: a ticket with its receipt stub attached.
precise: a move-only callable wrapper whose call operator invokes the stored function and stores the result or the thrown exception in its shared state.
source: D1 of F2-41 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed group of threads that take tasks from a queue and run them, one after another.
analogy: four cooks who stay all evening and take tickets from the rail.
precise: a set of long-lived worker threads and a shared task queue; submitting a task enqueues it and returns a handle (here a future); workers block on a condition variable while the queue is empty.
source: D2 of F2-41 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much work each task does.
analogy: a ticket for "one grain of rice" versus "a pot of rice".
precise: the ratio of a task's useful work to the per-task overhead (queueing, synchronisation, wake-ups); too fine and overhead dominates, too coarse and load is unbalanced.
source: D3 of F2-41 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: all workers wait for tasks that are queued behind them, so nothing runs.
analogy: every cook waits for a sauce ticket that no free cook can pick up.
precise: a deadlock in which every worker of a bounded pool is blocked waiting for the result of a task that is still in the same pool's queue.
source: D2 of F2-41 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: more busy threads than CPU cores.
analogy: eight cooks for four stoves.
precise: running more runnable threads than hardware threads, so the operating system time-slices them; adds context switches and cache disruption without adding throughput for CPU-bound work.
source: D3 of F2-41 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: some thread always makes progress, even if others are paused at any moment.
analogy: if one waiter freezes mid-reach, the others can still take plates.
precise: a progress guarantee: in any execution, if threads keep taking steps, some operation completes in a finite number of steps; no thread's suspension can block the others (unlike a lock, whose holder can be descheduled).
source: D15 of F2-42 (Maurice Herlihy, Nir Shavit, "The Art of Multiprocessor Programming") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every thread finishes its operation in a bounded number of its own steps.
analogy: each cook has their own mark and never retries.
precise: a stronger progress guarantee than lock-free: every operation completes in a bounded number of steps of the calling thread, whatever the others do.
source: D15 of F2-42 (Maurice Herlihy, Nir Shavit, "The Art of Multiprocessor Programming") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a thread finishes if it is left to run alone for long enough.
analogy: a waiter gets his plate if nobody else reaches at the same time.
precise: every operation completes if its thread eventually runs in isolation; weaker than lock-free (contending threads may keep undoing each other: livelock).
source: D15 of F2-42 (Maurice Herlihy, Nir Shavit, "The Art of Multiprocessor Programming") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circular buffer for exactly one writer thread and one reader thread, without locks.
analogy: the pass with the chef's mark and the waiter's mark.
precise: a bounded queue in which the producer alone writes the tail index and the consumer alone writes the head index; each publishes progress with a release store and reads the other's with an acquire load.
source: D2 of F2-42 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a linked-list stack where push and pop change the top pointer with compare-and-swap.
analogy: "I take the top plate only if it is still the one I saw".
precise: the lock-free LIFO stack published by R. K. Treiber (1986); push and pop retry a CAS on the head pointer.
source: D16 of F2-42 (R. Kent Treiber, "Systems Programming: Coping with Parallelism") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a value changes from A to B and back to A, and a compare-and-swap cannot tell.
analogy: plate X is on top, gone, and back on top; the waiter thinks nothing happened.
precise: a CAS succeeds because the location holds the expected value, although the state it stood for has changed in between (for example because a node was freed or reused and its address appears again).
source: D2 of F2-42 (Anthony Williams, "C++ Concurrency in Action") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: deciding when a removed node can be freed, given that another thread may still be reading it.
analogy: you may wash a plate only when no waiter is still looking at it.
precise: schemes such as hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation and read-copy-update (RCU) that defer freeing until no thread can hold a reference; without one, lock-free structures with removal must leak or risk use-after-free and ABA.
source: D3 of F2-42 (Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?"); D17 of F2-42 (Maged M. Michael, "Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: A checker built into the program that stops it when it touches memory it should not.
analogy: A kitchen inspector who stops service the moment a cook reaches into the wrong shelf.
precise: A compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) that adds checks around memory accesses and prints a report (kind of error, address, stack of calls, where the memory was allocated) before aborting.
source: D3 of F2-05, R6 of F2-05 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1)

simple: the part of a job that cannot be shared out limits how much faster more workers can make it.
analogy: one chef must still plate every dessert.
precise: if a fraction p of the run time can be spread perfectly over N processors, speed-up = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N), never more than 1 / (1 − p).
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the hardware's way of making sure cores do not keep using old copies of a value another core changed.
analogy: when one chef changes the board, everyone else's photo of it is torn up.
precise: a protocol that keeps the private caches' copies of each memory location consistent, usually by invalidating other copies before a write; it orders accesses to one location but does not make a read-then-write sequence indivisible.
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: A sentence about a process that stays true at every step.
analogy: "the two jars together hold twenty marbles", whatever moves are made.
precise: a condition (a Boolean expression about the state, F0-27) that holds in the starting state and is preserved by every allowed step, so it holds in every state reached.
source: W1 of F0-28 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-28 (title only, pending verification)
last_verified: not yet verified (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rules for which values loads may return when several cores read and write memory.
analogy: the kitchen's rules for when a note counts as "on the board".
precise: a specification of the allowed behaviours of a multithreaded program's loads and stores, across all memory locations, as defined for a hardware architecture or a programming language.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one chip with several complete processors (cores) on it.
analogy: several head chefs, each with their own line, sharing a pantry.
precise: a chip containing two or more cores, each with its own pipeline and registers (and usually its own first-level caches), that share memory and usually some caches.
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small queue in each core where finished stores wait before they are written to the cache.
analogy: each cook's outbox tray.
precise: a per-core FIFO of committed stores not yet written to the coherent cache; the core's own loads check it first (forwarding), while other cores cannot see its contents.
source: D4 of F1-37 (Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill and Wood, "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Something the C++ rules do not allow, where the program may then do anything.
analogy: A recipe step the kitchen rules forbid; nobody promises what happens if a cook does it anyway.
precise: Behaviour for which the standard imposes no requirements; the program may seem to work, give wrong answers or crash.
source: D2 of F2-02 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1)
